Whiplash-associated disorders: assessment and rehabilitation overview

By the editorial team | 9 min read | Tweet Share on LinkedIn

Whiplash-associated disorders describe the range of symptoms that follow a rapid acceleration-deceleration movement of the neck, most often in a road traffic collision. Neck pain and stiffness are the commonest complaints, but headache, dizziness, visual disturbance and arm symptoms also occur.

Grading and recovery

A widely used grading system runs from grade zero, with no neck complaint, to grade four, which indicates a fracture or dislocation. Most people seen in primary care have grade one or two. The expected course is favourable: a large share improve within the first three months, although a substantial minority report persistent pain and disability after a year.

Factors that predict a slower recovery

High initial pain intensity, high initial disability, neurological signs, fear of movement, pain catastrophising and low expectations of recovery are consistently linked to a poorer outcome. Psychological and social factors matter at least as much as the physical findings, so they belong in the very first assessment.

Clinical assessment

A structured assessment covers the mechanism of injury, pain behaviour, cervical range of motion, deep neck flexor endurance, motor control, sensation, balance, proprioception and function. Validated questionnaires such as the neck disability index give a baseline against which progress can be measured.

Red flags that call for urgent medical referral include suspected fracture, progressive neurological deficit, sudden severe headache, persistent visual problems, difficulty swallowing or speaking, and signs suggesting vascular involvement.

Management supported by evidence

Advice and reassurance, an early return to normal activity and active exercise form the core of care. Rest and prolonged collar use are discouraged because they tend to prolong symptoms. Exercise programmes that combine active mobility, motor control of the deep neck muscles, progressive strengthening and proprioceptive retraining have the best support.

Manual therapy can give short-term relief when it accompanies exercise; on its own its value is limited. Passive modalities such as ultrasound or electrotherapy add little once exercise and education are in place.
